text: Every large language model is built by stacking one unit, over and over, called the transformer block. GPT two small stacks twelve of them, and the largest models stack many more, but each block has the same design. It has two halves. In the first, the tokens exchange information through attention. In the second, each token thinks on its own, through a small neural network. Around both halves sit two supporting ideas you met earlier in the course, residual connections and layer normalisation, and this lesson puts all four pieces together.

It helps to picture a seminar. In the discussion phase, everyone listens to the others and updates their notes, and that is attention: communication between positions. Then comes a phase of private reflection, where each person works through their own notes without looking at anyone else's. That is the feed forward network, often called the MLP, which applies exactly the same small network to every token separately. Attention moves information around, and the MLP processes it where it lands.

The MLP itself is the two layer network from the neural networks module. It first widens each token's vector, usually to four times the model width, applies a smooth nonlinearity called GELU, which behaves like a softened ReLU, and then projects back down to the original width. Widening gives the network room to combine features in many ways before compressing the result again. Interpretability research suggests that a good deal of what a model knows about the world is stored in these layers.

Neither half replaces its input. Each one computes an update, and the update is added to the vector it started from, which is the residual connection. Think of a shared notebook that travels through the whole stack: every attention layer and every MLP reads the notebook and then writes a note into it, but nothing is ever erased. This running sum is called the residual stream. Because the additions pass gradients straight through, even a very deep stack can be trained, which is the same lesson residual networks taught in the vision module.

Before each half reads the stream, its input passes through layer normalisation. For every token separately, it subtracts the mean of the vector's entries and divides by their standard deviation, so the vector is centred with a spread of one, and then applies a learned scale and shift. This keeps the numbers in a healthy range no matter how many notes have piled up in the stream. GPT two places the normalisation before each half, which is called pre norm, while the original transformer placed it after, and pre norm turned out to train more reliably in deep stacks.

Written out, a block is just two lines. The stream x becomes x plus attention of the normalised x, and then x plus the MLP of the normalised x. Follow the shapes and you find the most important property of the design: a block takes a matrix of T rows and d columns and returns a matrix of exactly the same shape. Only inside the MLP does the width briefly grow to four times d. Because input and output match, blocks can be stacked as deep as we like, each one refining the same stream.

Now the whole model fits on one screen. Token embeddings plus position vectors form the initial stream. A stack of identical blocks refines it, layer by layer, with attention gathering context and the MLPs processing it. A final layer normalisation tidies the stream, and one last matrix maps each token's vector to a score for every word in the vocabulary. Each block has its own weights, so the stack is not one block repeated, but many blocks that share a design.

What comes out at the top is a vector of scores for every position, one score for each possible next token. In the final lesson of this module we turn those scores into probabilities, and then into actual text, by choosing the next token with temperature and top k sampling.
